title: JWST measures the most distant known ultra-cold Y dwarf
freshness: Unreviewed preprint first listed November 6, 2026; preferred 15-day search window.
excerpt: Five epochs of JWST imaging have pinned down the distance to JADES-GS-BD-5, an object colder than many ovens and about 64 parsecs away. It is roughly three times farther than any other Y dwarf with a reliable parallax distance.
whyItMatters: A geometric distance turns an unusually faint point of light into a useful test of how isolated, planetary-mass objects cool and how their atmospheres move heat and chemicals.

exploreFurther.label: Liu et al. preprint on arXiv

body:
## A cold neighbor hiding in a galaxy survey

JADES-GS-BD-5 is not a distant galaxy, even though astronomers found it in a survey designed to study distant galaxies. It is a nearby Y dwarf: a small, free-floating object too low in mass to sustain the hydrogen fusion that powers ordinary stars. A new analysis of repeated James Webb Space Telescope images places it about 64 parsecs, or 209 light-years, from Earth. That makes it roughly three times farther away than the previous most distant Y dwarfs with reliable geometric distances.

The result comes from parallax, the same effect that makes a nearby finger appear to jump against the background when you alternate between your left and right eyes. As Earth and JWST move around the Sun, a nearby object traces a tiny annual loop against much more distant sources. The size of that loop reveals the distance without relying on an atmospheric model.

The team used 50 JWST/NIRCam exposures grouped into five observing epochs across 2.03 years. After calibrating the positions against hundreds of reference sources, they measured a parallax of 15.7 milliarcseconds, with uncertainties of plus 1.4 and minus 1.3 milliarcseconds. The detection has a signal-to-noise ratio of 11.5. They also measured the object's motion across the sky at 49.8 milliarcseconds per year. Together, the distance and motion imply a sideways speed of about 15 kilometers per second, consistent with an object in the Milky Way's thin disk.

## A planet-like object that formed on its own

The measured distance fixes the object's true luminosity. JADES-GS-BD-5 radiates only about one ten-millionth of the Sun's power and is classified later than spectral type Y1, although the authors caution that the classification sequence is poorly mapped at this cold end.

Evolutionary models translate that faintness into a mass near eight times Jupiter's and an effective temperature around 300 kelvin, about 27 degrees Celsius. More than 90 percent of the modelled mass range falls below 13 Jupiter masses. Those numbers do not mean it is a planet orbiting a star. The team found no plausible stellar host, no clear close companion, and no significant acceleration suggesting an unseen binary partner. It is better described as an isolated planetary-mass brown dwarf, probably born through the same fragmentation process that makes stars.

Mass and temperature are inferred rather than directly measured. They depend on cooling models and on an assumed distribution of ages, while the parallax distance is geometric. The paper is also a preprint submitted to MNRAS and has not yet completed peer review.

The atmosphere presents a second puzzle. None of the tested model families reproduces the complete spectrum and photometry well. Models with disequilibrium chemistry and vertical mixing perform better, meaning gases may be carried between atmospheric layers faster than reactions can restore chemical balance. Water clouds or reduced water absorption could matter too, but the noisy, low-resolution spectrum does not establish that.

JWST found this object almost by accident while staring deeply into the GOODS-South field. Repeated deep-field observations could now build a sample of similarly cold wanderers far beyond the small volume surveyed by earlier infrared missions, giving astronomers more real atmospheres against which to test their models.
